At GS Construction, Sung Nak-hyun, Head of the Procurement Headquarters, was promoted to vice president. Vice President Sung has accumulated expertise in procurement over more than 30 years and was recognized for his achievements in cost reduction, digitalization of procurement processes, and mutual growth with partners. He is expected to focus on strengthening the company's cost competitiveness and project execution capabilities going forward. Most notably, GS Group expanded the scale of new executive appointments aimed at cultivating the next generation of management. In this reshuffle, 24 individuals were newly appointed as executive vice presidents, a 33.3% increase compared to 18 in each of the two previous regular executive appointments. Among the newly appointed executive vice presidents, eight are in their 40s, accounting for one-third of the total. GS Construction appointed 10 individuals as executive vice presidents, double the number from the previous appointment. It selected talent not only in core businesses such as housing and urban redevelopment but also in future business areas like development and data centers. GS EPS appointed a new executive vice president in his 40s as Head of the Future Business Division under the Power Policy Headquarters to respond to changes in electricity market regulations and advance new business initiatives. A GS official said, "Given significant domestic and international uncertainty, we have maintained stability while continuing the business innovations pursued by major subsidiaries." The official added, "Going forward, we will support each subsidiary in strengthening profitability and competitiveness in their core areas and identifying new growth drivers based on inter-subsidiary cooperation to create tangible results." title: Energy Materials Moves to Shut Down; No. 2 Shareholder Threatens Legal Action - Seoul Economic Daily
content:
Genesis PE, Which Invested 95 Billion Won, Pushes Back
Confirmed Liquidation Would Send Shockwaves Through Capital Markets This article appeared on Signal, a capital markets service, at 1:42 p.m. on Nov. 25, 2026. GS E&C (006360) is moving to shut down Energy Materials, its battery recycling subsidiary, following an indefinite suspension of operations last month. Genesis Private Equity, the second-largest shareholder in Energy Materials, has begun legal action, calling the move a unilateral decision made without its consent. The case could effectively wipe out the private equity firm's investment at the hands of a large corporate group, a prospect expected to send ripples through the capital market. GS E&C has settled on closing Energy Materials and plans to convene the subsidiary's board this week to approve the decision, according to investment banking sources on the 25th. Energy Materials, a GS E&C subsidiary, had been running large losses amid a weak market and falling metal prices. Genesis PE has escalated its legal action against Energy Materials. Early this month it filed for an injunction to suspend the effect of the suspension resolution, and it subsequently filed a main lawsuit arguing that the board resolution approving the shutdown was invalid, according to sources. The firm is understood to believe that the directors served only the interests of GS E&C, the largest shareholder, failing to treat shareholders equitably, and that there were procedural defects in convening the board meeting that decided on the suspension. Industry officials say that if the closure is confirmed, Genesis PE will find it difficult to recover its investment. Even if liquidation proceeds, GS E&C, now a creditor, would be paid first. Some point out that a precedent in which a large group winds down a subsidiary that had taken outside investment, leaving the investor with losses, could also dent confidence in GS Group across the capital market. The Energy Materials board had earlier voted last month to offer voluntary retirement to all employees and to suspend operations indefinitely. The Korea Development Bank then issued notice of a planned event of default, citing credit deterioration from the suspension, and GS E&C repaid 112.5 billion won in KDB loans on behalf of Energy Materials. The concern was that the subsidiary's loans could trigger a chain of defaults on the parent company's foreign currency bonds. Genesis PE invested 95 billion won in 2024 to acquire convertible preferred shares in Energy Materials. GS E&C currently holds 77.65% and Genesis PE 22.35%. The shareholders' agreement signed at the time of the investment is said to have required Genesis PE's prior consent for any suspension of business, dissolution or liquidation. There have been cases in which financial investors backing large corporate groups saw returns fall short of expectations or struggled to exit, but it is rare for a decision by the invested company itself to inflict large losses on the investment. "Large groups have shouldered as much of financial investors' principal as possible, driven less by the numbers than by a desire to preserve the trust of the market and institutional investors," an investment banking industry official said. "This decision will set a bad precedent for investing alongside large groups." Original reporting by Lee Young-ho for Seoul Economic Daily. AI-translated from Korean. title: GS Retail CEO Heo Seohong Promoted to President; Recognized for Strengthening Core Business Competitiveness - 아시아경제

GS Retail CEO Heo Seohong Promoted to President; Recognized for Strengthening Core Business Competitiveness Heo Seohong, CEO and president of GS Retail, has been promoted from vice president to president just two years after taking office. On November 25, GS Group announced that Heo Seohong, CEO of GS Retail, had been promoted from vice president to president in its “2027 Regular Executive Appointments.” Heo Seohong, CEO and President of GS Retail. GS25 pursued a “scrap-and-build” strategy focused on improving the profitability of existing stores rather than expanding its store count, while also increasing the number of stores with an expanded fresh-food offering. GS THE FRESH strengthened its competitiveness in the supermarket market through franchise-led growth and an enhanced quick-commerce business, while GS Shop continued to improve its performance by developing its own fashion brands and expanding its range of differentiated products. Heo plans to continue strengthening the competitiveness of core businesses, including convenience stores, supermarkets and home shopping, while laying the foundation for mid- to long-term growth by identifying new businesses and expanding overseas. He previously set a mid- to long-term target of achieving KRW 380 billion in operating profit by 2028. Heo began his career in 2002 as an analyst in the corporate finance division of Samjong KPMG and went on to work at the new business team of GS Home Shopping, Chevron and GS Energy, among others. title: BMW GS Rallye 2026 – Rain, Gravel and a Little GS That Could - Bike Rider Magazine
content: Nearly 160 riders, a weather forecast from hell and a route through the central North Island. Paul Lance heads to the BMW GS Rallye in Taupō aboard the new F 450 GS, discovering that you don’t need a massive adventure bike to have a massive amount of fun. There’s something rather satisfying about preparing for a big adventure ride. Getting the gear sorted, loading the GPS, checking the motorcycle and looking forward to a day exploring roads and tracks you’ve probably never ridden before. It’s even better when someone else has done all the hard work of finding the route. Unfortunately, there’s one thing the organisers of the BMW GS Rallye couldn’t control. And as I drove down to Taupō for the 2026 event, the forecast was becoming increasingly unpleasant. Heavy rain, thunderstorms and the sort of conditions that make you question whether spending an entire day on a motorcycle is really the best idea. By Saturday morning, those forecasts were proving depressingly accurate. The rain was absolutely hammering down, with nearly 160 riders preparing to head off into the countryside on everything from enormous BMW GS adventure tourers to smaller machines more suited to getting themselves into trouble. My motorcycle for the weekend was the new BMW F 450 GS Trophy, equipped with the clever Easy Ride Clutch system. I’d ridden the little BMW previously during our initial test, but this would be something different. A full day of road riding, gravel, forest tracks, mud, rain and whatever else the central North Island could throw at us. It was the sort of test that would reveal a lot more about the F 450 GS than another pleasant afternoon on dry gravel roads. And as it turned out, the little BMW was one of the stars of the weekend. This year’s GS Rallye was based at Wairakei Resort, just outside Taupō, with BMW Motorrad New Zealand taking a more direct role in organising the event. It was a slightly different approach from previous years. Rather than simply turning up for the ride and making your own accommodation arrangements, participants could book a package incorporating their accommodation, evening meals and breakfasts. That made the whole weekend feel more like a proper motorcycle rally, with everyone gathering in the same place rather than disappearing to accommodation scattered around the district. It also meant plenty of opportunities to catch up with familiar faces, meet new riders and discuss the various advantages of spending far too much money on adventure motorcycles. Moto Track and Trail helped plan and manage the riding, with routes supplied beforehand as GPX files. These could be loaded into a GPS unit or compatible navigation app, allowing riders to follow the route at their own pace. There were three main choices: a sealed-road ride, a gravel-focused route and a gravel route incorporating optional technical breakouts. The main adventure route would head north towards Ōtorohanga for lunch and fuel before making its way back towards Taupō. Having attended the previous GS Rallye, where we’d tackled plenty of gravel and some fairly challenging terrain, I’d initially been looking forward to the optional breakouts. But with the weather forecast deteriorating by the hour, I was beginning to reconsider that enthusiasm. Perhaps discretion really was the better part of valour. Then again, that would depend on how much fun everyone else appeared to be having. Saturday morning arrived with the sort of rain that makes you wonder whether you should be building an ark rather than preparing a motorcycle. Friends and family were sending me videos showing terrible conditions elsewhere in the country, and all that weather appeared to be heading directly towards Taupō. I decided there was no point taking chances with my riding gear. Over my usual Leatt adventure equipment went a set of Scott waterproofs, effectively adding another layer between me and the elements. I also treated the inside of my visor to help prevent fogging and applied a water-repellent product to the outside. The idea was simple: stay as dry as possible, keep the visor clear and hopefully avoid spending the day wondering whether my socks were turning into small aquariums. Once I reached the more technical tracks and needed to open my visor to see where I was going, rain found its way onto the inside. At that point, all the preparation in the world becomes rather academic. You can polish the outside of your visor as much as you like, but when there’s water running down the inside, visibility becomes considerably more interesting. Meanwhile, the rain showed absolutely no sign of giving up. I let the main group of motorcycles head off first so I could film the departure. Then I climbed aboard the F 450 GS and set off in pursuit, making sure I stayed ahead of the sweep rider. The first thing that struck me was how easy the BMW was to ride. It’s a compact motorcycle, with a narrow waist, accessible riding position and very little of the bulk you associate with the larger GS models. On my test bike, I could put both feet firmly on the ground. That’s reassuring when you’re setting off into unknown terrain, particularly with the weather doing its best to make everything slippery. I’d fitted a Quad Lock phone mount to the handlebars, downloaded BMW’s Motorrad Connected app to my iPhone and paired the phone with the bike’s TFT dashboard via Bluetooth. That let me follow the route using navigation information on the BMW’s display, which was particularly useful when exploring unfamiliar roads. Unfortunately, as I would discover later, having a route displayed on a screen doesn’t necessarily prevent you from getting lost. The opening part of the route included rather more sealed road than I’d expected. Compared with the previous year’s event, which had featured extensive gravel riding and some quite challenging sections, this route was clearly designed to be more accessible. And looking around at the enormous variety of motorcycles taking part, I could understand why. There were plenty of large-capacity GS models, many carrying enough accessories to fund a reasonable family holiday. Their owners weren’t necessarily looking to throw them down a slippery hillside or spend half the day digging them out of a bog. Not everyone who owns an adventure motorcycle wants to compete in the International Six Days Enduro. Eventually I arrived at one of the optional technical sections. A marshal was stationed at the entrance, and I asked what the track was like. Nothing too difficult, apparently. Just a straightforward bit of riding through the bush. The good news was that the volcanic soil around Taupō drains remarkably well. Despite the torrential rain, we weren’t riding through endless deep mud, although the tracks were certainly slippery enough to demand concentration. The route wound through tight forest trails, climbing and descending between trees before reaching a short hill with a corner partway up. A couple of larger motorcycles became stuck, and before long there was a queue of bikes waiting to get through. Eventually we reached another group of riders standing beside a locked gate. Apparently, in dry conditions it would have been fairly straightforward. In the rain, however, even some of the more experienced riders were struggling to get up it. The organisers had sensibly decided to divert everyone through the gate instead. “When the marshal arrived to unlock it, he dropped the key into the long grass. And couldn’t find it.” When the marshal arrived to unlock it, he dropped the key into the long grass. Unfortunately, a small group of us ended up following a track that seemed to become progressively less used, until we were negotiating fallen branches, logs, long grass and narrow trails that didn’t look as though they’d seen a motorcycle in years. At some point we collectively decided that perhaps we weren’t heading in quite the right direction. Turning around eventually brought us back to other riders, and after a little more exploring we finally found our way out. The whole episode was a reminder that adventure riding doesn’t always go to plan. But it also demonstrated just how manageable the little BMW was in difficult conditions. I’d previously experienced BMW’s Easy Ride Clutch during our original F 450 GS test, but a day like this was an excellent opportunity to find out whether the system offered any real benefit. The system uses a centrifugal clutch that engages automatically as engine speed rises, meaning you can pull away without operating the clutch lever. Combined with BMW’s Shift Assistant Pro, you can also change up and down through the six-speed gearbox without touching the clutch. But throughout most of the Rallye, I simply didn’t bother. “And after spending most of the day without touching the clutch lever, I was thoroughly convinced of its benefits.” Initially, I’d wondered whether needing to bring the engine above approximately 2500rpm to engage the clutch might make the rear wheel more likely to spin in slippery conditions. The engagement was smooth and progressive, with plenty of traction available even on wet gravel and forest tracks. It was particularly useful when negotiating technical sections, where the last thing you want is to be constantly juggling the clutch while trying to maintain balance and find traction. Even when crossing small logs or obstacles, I found myself simply using the throttle rather than deliberately slipping the clutch. The system isn’t a substitute for riding technique, and there will be situations where experienced off-road riders prefer manual clutch control. But for the kind of adventure riding we were doing, it made life considerably easier. And after spending most of the day without touching the clutch lever, I was thoroughly convinced of its benefits. The F 450 GS is powered by a newly developed 420cc parallel-twin producing a claimed 35kW (48hp) and 43Nm. With a ready-to-ride weight of 178kg in standard specification, it sits at the lighter end of BMW’s adventure range. The engine uses a 135-degree crankpin arrangement, giving it a distinctive character, while the compact chassis incorporates a tubular steel frame, 19-inch front and 17-inch rear wheels, and 180mm of suspension travel at both ends. There’s a substantial electronics package, too, including riding modes, traction control and ABS Pro. My test bike was the GS Trophy version, wearing its Racing blue metallic paintwork with red and white details. It also came equipped with features particularly relevant to a day like this, including handguards, enduro footrests, an aluminium bashplate and a taller tinted screen. For the Rallye, I selected Enduro mode and disabled the rear ABS. That was pretty much where I left the settings for the entire day. The system reduced traction-control intervention and gave me enough freedom to move the rear wheel around on gravel without constantly fighting the electronics. In Enduro mode, the initial response felt a little softer than I’d ideally like. Personally, I prefer a slightly more immediate throttle when riding enthusiastically on gravel, particularly when using the rear wheel to help steer the motorcycle. In fact, once I started enjoying the flowing gravel sections, I was surprised by just how easily I could slide the little BMW through corners. You don’t necessarily need enormous horsepower to have fun on gravel. Sometimes having a lighter motorcycle with accessible performance is much more entertaining. The F 450 GS made that point repeatedly throughout the day. After escaping the forest tracks, the route continued north towards Ōtorohanga. There were more sealed roads, more gravel and, at one point, a navigation system that seemed determined to send me somewhere entirely different. I found myself following a sealed road with the GPS suggesting I had another 43km to travel before turning. Eventually I stopped, studied the route and realised I’d wandered away from the intended track. A little retracing soon had me back where I belonged. “You don’t necessarily need enormous horsepower to have fun on gravel.” Long, flowing, undulating stretches where you could see well ahead, settle into a rhythm and simply enjoy the way the motorcycle moved beneath you. Despite its modest power output, there was enough performance to accelerate strongly out of corners and use the rear wheel to help steer. The narrow chassis made it easy to move the bike around beneath me, and I actually spent much of the gravel riding sitting down. Rather than fighting the motorcycle or constantly shifting my weight, I could simply guide it into corners, let the rear move a little and drive out the other side. The BMW has a single 310mm front disc with a four-piston Brembo caliper, and there’s plenty of stopping power available. With the GPS warning of a junction a couple of hundred metres ahead, I could leave the braking reasonably late and trust the system to slow the motorcycle effectively. That combination of light weight, accurate handling and strong brakes made the F 450 GS exceptionally confidence-inspiring. Eventually we reached Ōtorohanga, where the organisers had arranged for a local café to accommodate the incoming riders. There were motorcycles everywhere, with riders grabbing coffee, sandwiches, fuel and a chance to warm up. I headed for the petrol station, filled the BMW and sorted out some supplies before continuing. One of my smarter decisions had been packing a second pair of waterproof gloves. By lunchtime, the first pair was thoroughly soaked. It’s remarkable how much better you feel when your hands are warm and dry. Unfortunately, that doesn’t necessarily apply to the rest of your body. Despite the waterproof gear, water was gradually finding its way into places it really had no business being. And as it turned out, the afternoon would provide some of the best sections of the entire Rallye. After lunch, the route opened up into some truly superb gravel riding. There were long, sweeping roads with smooth surfaces, flowing bends and undulations that made the ride feel almost effortless. Fourth, fifth and occasionally sixth gear, with the BMW moving gently beneath me as I flowed from one corner to the next. There was enough traction to get on the throttle early, enough power to make things entertaining and not so much weight that the motorcycle felt like hard work. Eventually we entered another forest section, where the tracks became more overgrown and the riding a little more technical. There were large holes filled with water, fallen branches and a few places where choosing the right line became rather important. This was also where the BMW’s suspension limitations became more apparent. The F 450 GS has 180mm of suspension travel, but it’s an adventure motorcycle rather than a dedicated enduro bike. The suspension is deliberately controlled rather than extremely soft and plush, which helps make it such a good road motorcycle. But hit a particularly deep hole or sharp obstacle and you’re reminded that there’s only so much suspension travel available. I found myself standing on the footpegs more often through these sections, using my legs to absorb the bigger impacts. And while there wasn’t enough power to effortlessly lift the front wheel over obstacles with a twist of the throttle, a little body movement and careful application of power usually did the job. There was no need to worry about stalling or constantly covering the clutch lever. Eventually the gravel gave way to more sealed roads, and we began making our way back towards Taupō. A few other riders caught up, and we enjoyed a spirited run through some excellent winding roads. The little BMW was just as entertaining on the tarmac as it had been on gravel. There were only a handful of motorcycles ahead of us, although some riders had chosen the sealed-road route or may have returned earlier. Over the following hour, more bikes began arriving. There were plenty of tired faces, dirty motorcycles and riders who looked as though they’d enjoyed themselves enormously. Fortunately, the weather had improved during the afternoon, allowing us to dry out a little before returning. Peeling off the waterproof layers revealed the usual problems. My boots had leaked, which meant my socks were wet. The moisture had then worked its way up into the bottom of my trousers. Meanwhile, water running down my neck tube had found its way into my shirt. The waterproof outer layers had done a pretty good job, but water is remarkably inventive when it comes to finding a way inside your clothing. I was also beginning to appreciate the BMW’s heated grips, which I’d discovered partway through the day. A particularly welcome feature when your gloves have spent several hours pretending to be dishcloths. By the time we returned, I’d covered close to 450km across a mixture of sealed roads, gravel and forest tracks. That’s a substantial day on any adventure motorcycle, particularly in conditions like those we’d encountered. It has enough performance to make the bike entertaining without constantly demanding attention, and the smooth power delivery makes it easy to find traction on slippery surfaces. The chassis is wonderfully manageable, with a riding position that gives you confidence and a narrow shape that makes it easy to move around. The front brake is particularly impressive, while the suspension strikes a useful compromise between road comfort and off-road ability. At 182cm tall, I found the riding position a little cramped after such a long day, and my backside was beginning to complain by the time we reached Wairakei. But then we’d spent the best part of a day riding nearly 450km, much of it in fairly demanding conditions. I’d probably have been uncomfortable on just about anything by that stage. The suspension also reminds you that this isn’t a hardcore enduro motorcycle when the terrain gets particularly rough. The F 450 GS is an accessible, versatile adventure bike that’s capable of taking riders well beyond ordinary sealed roads. And with the Easy Ride Clutch, it’s one of the most approachable motorcycles of its kind. Looking back on the weekend, I think BMW deserves considerable credit for the event. The weather could easily have turned it into a miserable experience, yet the organisers managed to keep everything running and provide a memorable day for a large group of riders. The route was certainly more road-focused than I’d expected. Personally, I’d have preferred a little more gravel, particularly given how good the afternoon sections were. But that needs to be considered in the context of who was attending. There were riders of varying abilities, on motorcycles ranging from smaller adventure machines to very large, expensive GS models. “You really don’t need a massive adventure motorcycle to have a massive adventure.” I spoke to a couple of riders who’d attended the previous event and had found the technical terrain so demanding that they’d only managed to reach the lunch stop before deciding to return. That tells you something about the challenges of organising an event like this. Make it too difficult, and some riders won’t enjoy themselves. Make it too easy, and the more experienced riders may feel they’ve missed out on an adventure. The optional breakouts were a sensible solution, allowing riders to choose additional challenges without forcing everyone into difficult terrain. Had the weather been better, I’m sure those sections would have been particularly enjoyable. The other thing I liked was seeing motorcycles from other manufacturers taking part. Alongside the BMWs were KTMs, Yamaha Ténérés and other adventure bikes. At the end of the day, the point isn’t simply to promote one brand. It’s to get riders out enjoying their motorcycles, exploring new places and meeting people who share the same enthusiasm. And judging by the tired but happy faces returning to Wairakei, BMW achieved exactly that. I went into the BMW GS Rallye expecting a good day’s riding and an opportunity to spend more time with the new F 450 GS. There was torrential rain, slippery forest tracks, a missing gate key, some navigational confusion and some of the best flowing gravel roads I’ve ridden in a while. And through it all, the little BMW was outstanding. I’d already been impressed by the F 450 GS during our original test, but a long day in genuinely challenging conditions confirmed just how capable it is. The Easy Ride Clutch was particularly impressive, removing one more thing to worry about when riding technical terrain and making the motorcycle exceptionally easy to manage. There were times when I wished for slightly sharper throttle response in Enduro mode and a little more suspension compliance over bigger obstacles. But those are relatively minor criticisms of a motorcycle that managed everything I asked of it. And the whole experience reinforced something I’ve been thinking for a while. You really don’t need a massive adventure motorcycle to have a massive adventure. Sometimes a smaller, lighter bike is exactly what you want. Especially when it’s pouring with rain, you’re halfway up a slippery forest track and somebody’s lost the key to the gate. All the latest motorcycle news from New Zealand and around the globe. title: GS Retail stock enters Cambodia through GS25 franchise deal - ad-hoc-news.de
content: GS Retail is expanding the GS25 convenience-store chain into Cambodia through a master franchise agreement with Meta Retail. The first flagship store opened in Phnom Penh on November 23, according to Inside Retail Asia. The partners plan to build a 500-store network over the next decade. The Phnom Penh flagship covers 400 square meters and carries about 3,000 products, including GS25 private-label brands Youus and Real Price. The agreement follows a year of due diligence and joint review between GS Retail and Meta Retail. GS25 has entered Cambodia after expanding in Vietnam and Mongolia. Inside Retail Asia reports that the chain has more than 450 stores in Vietnam and over 280 locations in Mongolia, giving the Cambodian launch an established regional operating base. The overseas rollout comes as South Korea's convenience-store market matures. A November 19 industry comparison by Top Daily placed GS25 alongside BGF Retail's CU, Seven Eleven and Emart24 as the country's four major chains. The report said CU and GS25 were pursuing expansion, while Seven Eleven and Emart24 were emphasizing efficiency and profitability. GS Retail is headquartered in Seoul and operates consumer businesses including GS25 convenience stores, GS The Fresh supermarkets and GS Shop home shopping. Its domestic convenience-store activities compete most directly with BGF Retail's CU, while Seven Eleven and Emart24 remain other national-format rivals. South Korea's retail environment remains the immediate operating backdrop for GS Retail, alongside the company's international expansion into Southeast Asia. title: Speaker G S Patil summons Forest officials over elephant relocation row - Deccan Herald
content: Speaker of the Legislative Assembly G S Patil has summoned officials of the Forest Department for a meeting on Wednesday to discuss the relocation of elephants from Belur in Hassan district to the Bhadra Tiger Reserve Chikkamagaluru after legislators from the latter district threatened to resign over the development. Mudigere MLA Nayana Motamma submitted her resignation to the Speaker's office on Monday in a sign of protest. However, she did accompany Chikkamagaluru MLA H D Thammaiah and Tarikere MLA G H Srinivas to the meeting with Patil, who was apprised of the situation. Motamma said that the Speaker was convening a meeting of the Forest Department officials and four MLAs, including Sringeri MLA T D Rajegowda, whose constituency will also be impacted by the relocation operation. "The Speaker was surprised to learn that the foresters had undertaken the operation without taking the legislators, planters' association and farmers into confidence," Motamma said. Accusing the Forest Department of entirely disregarding the safety of the people of Chikkamagaluru, Motamma asked, "Who will be held responsible for any loss of life during the operation? What is the guarantee these relocated elephants will not stray into human habitats later." Chief Minister D K Shivakumar, who is currently touring Japan, is learnt to have spoken to the Chikkamagaluru legislators, and asked them to keep their resignation in abeyance, while promising them that the issue would be resolved. "The CM has instructed the Forest Department to put the operation on hold till he returns to Bengaluru on Wednesday night," said Motamma. Disputing the foresters' claims that the elephants had moved to the Bhadra Tiger Reserve of their own accord, Motamma said, "They were driven there to ease the pressure on the forest in Hassan. But our district is already grappling with human-animal conflict given that there are around 400 elephants in the region." Meanwhile, KPCC president B K Hariprasad urged Nayana Motamma to reconsider her decision to resign, saying the issue would be resolved through discussions with the government. He said the MLA had agreed to hold back her resignation for now and that a decision would be taken after the chief minister returns from Japan.

title: Choi Ga-eun Ties Career High in GS Caltex Victory - 조선일보
content: Middle blocker's 15 points and '50% mindset' lead team to first-round finish [Daejeon = Sports Chosun Reporter Lee Jong-seo] "When I think I need to do well, I end up performing worse." Choi Ga-eun, 25 years old (GS Caltex), tied her personal best score with 15 points in the first-round match against Jung Kwan Jang Red Sparrows in the HK Insurance 2026-2027 V-League women's division, held at Chungmu Gymnasium in Daejeon on November 24. She also recorded a personal best of 4 points from serves and 5 blocks. GS Caltex, led by Choi Ga-eun's performance, defeated Jung Kwan Jang with a set score of 3-1 and finished the first round in first place. After the match, Choi Ga-eun said, "It was the last game of the first round, and I’m glad we could finish in first place. There were difficult moments, but it was good that the players overcame them." This season has started well. In 3 out of 6 games in the first round, she scored double-digit points, and she consistently recorded blocks in every game. She has firmly established herself as the team’s starting middle blocker. Lee Young-taek, GS Caltex’s head coach, also smiles and says, "She is doing well," but adds a word of caution: "While I give appropriate praise, getting too excited when things go well can have a negative effect." Choi Ga-eun, along with Kwon Min-ji, is a 'mood maker' for GS Caltex. Her bright energy injects vitality into the team, but there’s a concern that if she gets too excited, she might become unstable. The coach said, "I lightly point out things when needed to help her manage her mind. (Choi) Ga-eun has bright energy, but sometimes she rushes too much. I talk to her about those aspects." Choi Ga-eun seemed aware of the coach’s intentions. Regarding the coach’s advice, she laughed and said, "He gives me more whips than carrots," adding, "It has a good influence in filling my shortcomings." She also has her own unique 'mantra': "Do 50%." She explained, "If I get greedy and try too hard, it doesn’t work. When things don’t go well, self-blame grows bigger. So I enter the game comfortably, thinking, ‘Just do 50% of what I prepared.’ My performance comes out well, and even when things don’t go smoothly, I can let it go." She added, "In games where my condition is bad or I feel pressured, if I think, ‘I must do well,’ I can’t perform. I focus on helping and being helped well." The personal best-tying 15 points on November 24 were also born from the coach’s advice. Choi Ga-eun said, "With the team’s good performance and my own form, I had a desire for more points, but yesterday after training, the coach said, ‘If you sacrifice and help instead of being greedy for points, things will go well.’ I didn’t push for points and blended into the team, which led to scoring well." Her personal best of 4 serve points that day also came after letting go of greed. Choi Ga-eun said, "During the season preparation, we emphasized managing unforced errors. As a middle blocker, if I serve and make an error, I get replaced by the libero and lose the chance to recover. Instead of aiming for points, I focused on placing the serve where I intended, which led to positive results." Mindset isn’t everything. All of this was possible due to intense training. Choi Ga-eun recalled the off-season, saying, "The secret to this year’s performance is the high training volume. Even though we were champions, our vacation wasn’t long. Returning early and syncing with the players was the key."

title: European Stocks Are Forecast to Rise in 2027 Even as Earnings Growth Slows - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Analysis and forecasts on global economies and markets for the year ahead from economists and strategists across Goldman Sachs. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. European stocks are forecast to rise in 2027, but to post lower returns than their counterparts in the US and Asia, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Slower earnings growth, weaker economic growth, and high public deficits and energy prices are expected to weigh on European stocks, writes Sharon Bell, senior European equity strategist for Goldman Sachs Research. “That said, European equities continue to deliver positive performance, offer several attractive characteristics to global investors, and we expect continued positive flows especially from foreign investors,” Bell adds. Our strategists forecast a 9% total return for Europe’s STOXX 600 index over the next 12 months (as of November 13). European equity returns have historically tracked earnings growth expectations, and current estimates of growth in European earnings per share (EPS) are “consistent with positive but low returns” for stocks, Bell observes. That said, equity performance has already slowed significantly relative to earnings growth, she adds—the STOXX 600 is up around 10% in 2026 (as of November 23), even as company earnings are substantially higher than that. Next year, earnings growth is expected to slow to 7%, from 18% this year. “The slowdown is partly a function of Energy EPS decline and partly a function of weaker economic growth and margins next year as we see the impact of higher energy costs and rates feed through,” Bell writes. European stocks trade at a discount to their US counterparts, but that discount has narrowed substantially since late 2024. The discount as a proportion of stocks’ price/earnings ratios is now at 14% on a sector-adjusted basis, having once been as large as 34%. Since 2022, Germany’s DAX index and the UK’s FTSE 100 index have kept pace with the S&P 500 in terms of total returns, partly as a function of European stocks narrowing their valuation discount against US peers. “Accordingly, we think that European indexes are likely to lag modestly over the next year given the valuation gap to the US is now smaller, and roughly in line with its history, and given that earnings growth is likely to be slower in Europe than in other regions,” Bell writes. Our strategists anticipate positive flows into European stocks next year, especially from foreign investors. Bell identifies several reasons why she expects global investors to continue allocating capital to the region: AI-diversification benefits: On average, European indexes—especially Switzerland’s SMI and the UK’s FTSE 100—have been resilient (and even risen) as artificial intelligence (AI) stocks decline. Relatively high free cash flow: High cash spending has eroded free cash flow for US companies, which also limits their ability to buy back their shares. This has happened at the same time as more IPOs and expiring lock-ups are increasing the net supply of stocks to the market, which can weigh on stock valuations. In contrast, free cash flow for European stocks remains relatively high, and buybacks remain strong. At the same time, M&A activity is robust, and a smaller volume of new stocks is coming to the market via IPOs in Europe. “In other words, shrinking net equity supply continues to support Europe regardless of investor allocations,” Bell explains. Keen international investors: Goldman Sachs Research already sees evidence of flows into European stocks from outside the continent. “We find global investors, especially from the US, are allocating increasing amounts to Europe, mainly via global and global ex-US funds, while domestic European investors still appear reluctant to allocate,” Bell writes. Energy prices will be key for European stocks in 2027. “European equities have the most to gain from relief on energy supply and prices (and, of course, the most to lose if this does not happen),” Bell writes. Goldman Sachs Research estimates that each 10% rise in the price of Brent crude oil takes around 1% off the valuations of European stocks. Our commodities strategists expect both Brent crude and European liquefied natural gas to decline in 2027 as suppliers adapt to disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil is forecast to fall to $78 per barrel by the end of 2027 from around $91.50 today (as of November 23). Some European sectors tend to perform better when energy prices fall. Cyclical stocks, German blue-chip companies in the DAX index, and consumer discretionary stocks would stand to benefit the most as gas prices decline, while energy, quality stocks, defensives, and the UK’s FTSE 100 index are all likely to be underperformers. “All other things being equal, lower energy prices through 2027 militate against shifting more towards quality or defensives in our allocation and push toward more cyclical exposure despite a likely window for weaker economic growth in Europe over the winter,” Bell writes. European corporate balance sheets are not stretched—Europe’s technology companies have exceptionally low debt—and stock valuations held up comparatively well when European government bond yields rose compared with their peers this year. At the same time, “it is difficult to argue that Europe equities can disentangle themselves from a broader sovereign risk event, especially banks and other domestic stocks,” Bell writes. While our economists do not forecast a sovereign risk event for 2027, the indebtedness of European governments undoubtedly remains a drag on growth, she adds. Historically, a 10-basis-point widening in the OAT-Bund spread, the premium that investors require for holding a French government bond rather than a comparable German government bond, has been associated with a decline of around 3% for France’s CAC 40 index of large-cap stocks and a decline of 4% for French domestic stocks. “We think it is too early to re-engage with French domestic stocks,” Bell writes. Her team prefers getting exposure to Germany and the DAX index, given relatively low valuations and continued fiscal spending by the German government, or to UK domestic stocks, which could benefit if UK government bond yields and energy prices fall next year. title: Japanese Stocks Are Projected to Rally Again in the Coming Year - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Analysis and forecasts on global economies and markets for the year ahead from economists and strategists across Goldman Sachs. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. The Japanese stock market’s gains this year have been driven largely by the banking and artificial intelligence (AI) sectors. Goldman Sachs Research expects the performance to broaden going forward, particularly because of the government’s push for corporations to use their cash to invest in growth. As long as capital expenditures in AI are ongoing, Japanese equity earnings per share (EPS) are forecast to increase again in fiscal year 2027—though at a more modest pace, Bruce Kirk, chief Japan equity strategist, writes in a report. Goldman Sachs Research projects the TOPIX of Japanese equities to rally about 20% to 4,500 in the next 12 months (as of November 24), based on estimates for growth in EPS of 9% in fiscal year 2027. “We believe that 2027 will be a transitional year for the Japanese equities market,” Kirk writes. The main drivers of Japanese stock gains for the past three years have been AI and normalization by the Bank of Japan. In 2027, Kirk expects investors’ tactical diversification into less crowded positions and less volatile themes, combined with the government’s market-wide efforts for corporations to invest sensibly in future growth, to produce a shift in the factors propelling the market. Communications from Japan’s Tokyo Stock Exchange; the Financial Services Agency; the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry; and the Takaichi administration suggest “a well-coordinated shift in top-down pressure towards promoting the use of excess cash reserves to drive the future growth initiatives across corporate Japan,” Kirk writes. “Growth” is the key word in Japan's corporate governance reforms, according to Goldman Sachs Research. “This should lead to a re-focus of interest on corporate governance-related themes in 2027, but skewed more towards growth investment and corporate restructuring,” Kirk writes. Our strategists have argued that improvement in return-on-equity at the index level will require “more drastic corporate structuring measures” than have taken place so far. These measures include mergers and acquisitions, operating segment restructuring, and consolidation. “This is where we think investor interest will shift towards in 2027,” Kirk writes. Goldman Sachs Research notes that, despite recent improvements, the TOPIX's return on equity still lags behind a wide range of markets globally. One of the best ways to address this gap would be to promote sector consolidation via increased levels of domestic mergers and acquisitions, Kirk writes. Prime Minister Takaichi's growth strategy highlights 17 strategic sectors and 62 key products and technologies. The strategy is designed to promote investments that enhance resilience against potential crises and promote growth, according to Goldman Sachs Research. “Without secure and reliable access to energy, power generation, natural resources, critical minerals, and rare earths, most of the other growth strategies will become almost impossible to achieve,” Kirk writes. As part of a $550 billion trade deal between the US and Japan, a number of power generation and energy security-related projects have already been approved or announced. “We see significant overlap between the Japanese government's energy and resource-related initiatives and future partnership opportunities with the US administration,” Kirk writes. Kirk identifies five key themes for investors in Japanese equities in 2027: AI innovation and quality: Goldman Sachs Research’s framework for AI-related stocks sorts them into two core groups: the AI semiconductor ecosystem and the AI data center hardware ecosystem. While the correlation between the two groups is “extremely high,” Kirk points out that AI companies in this dataset that scored highly in terms of innovation and quality significantly outperformed those that scored lower between April 2025 and June 2026. Corporate restructuring: Japan's new corporate governance code focuses on "growth-oriented governance." It urges corporate investment that supports sustainable mid- to long-term growth. It also stresses fair treatment of minority shareholders during mergers. Goldman Sachs Research expects a significant rise in takeover bids, management buyouts, and industry consolidation from 2027 onward. Physical AI: Labor costs for non-financial TOPIX companies reached 10.5% of sales in fiscal year 2025, up from 8.5% in fiscal year 2016. This is the highest level in a decade, excluding distortions during Covid. Goldman Sachs Research analysts forecast that humanoid robot prices, meanwhile, will decline from about $42,000 in 2025 to $21,000 by 2035. The government’s strategy aims for the deployment of 350,000 AI robots by 2030 and about 10 million by 2040. Energy and resource security: Japan imports almost all of its oil, natural gas, coal, and critical minerals. Its energy self-sufficiency fell from 22% in fiscal year 1998 to 6% after the shutdown of the Fukushima nuclear power station in 2011. While that figure recovered to 16% by 2024, Japan remains highly vulnerable to supply disruptions. The government's growth strategy aims to diversify sources of minerals and raw materials; secure energy supplies; strengthen the production supply chain for components; and expand solar, thermal, and advanced nuclear power. These plans could benefit trading companies, shipping firms, energy companies, and heavy industry. Cybersecurity: Japan's growth strategy explicitly prioritizes security products and services suited to the AI era, including support for domestic technology development and adoption. The government aims for domestic cybersecurity companies to generate annual revenue of more than 3 trillion yen ($18.8 billion) by 2035. title: This Acura Integra GS-R For Sale Is The 2 Fast 2 Furious Car Of Your Dreams - CarScoops
content: It's supercharged, dripping in red, and selling with no reserve. The Nissan Skyline, Mazda RX-7, and Toyota Supra were far from the only beloved Japanese sports cars used throughout the Fast and Furious franchise. During the first film, two Acura Integras were used, including one driven by Mia Toretto, played by Jordana Brewster. As it turns out, an Integra GS-R also served as an extra in "2 Fast 2 Furious" and is now up for auction in the U.S. The Bring a Trailer auction doesn't note if the car had any screen time, but documents from filming in 2002 show the production company behind the film was charged $2,472 for damage to the Integra's front and rear bumpers and grille. The year after serving as an extra, the car was repainted in a combination of black and red. This Integra certainly isn't as cool as Brian O'Conner's Nissan R34 Skyline GT-R, but it will be a lot more affordable, so it has that going for it. Contrasting the exterior paint is a set of 10-spoke 19-inch HRE wheels clad in 255/40 Firestone Firehawk tires. The Acura also includes a set of upgraded drilled-and-slotted brake discs and SSBC Force 10 calipers. It's under the hood where even more significant upgrades have been made. The original 1.8-liter inline-4 now includes a Jackson Racing supercharger and an aftermarket air intake. The listing doesn't make any mention of how much power the car has, though it's safe to assume it should be pretty sprightly. Drive is sent to the front wheels through a five-speed manual transmission. The engine bay also looks the part of a dramatic show car. It includes bright red hoses throughout, several chrome accents, and a red Comptech Sport strut bar. The wild red theme continues into the cabin, where the seats are trimmed in red and black, and there are red floor mats, a red instrument cluster, and red on the Momo steering wheel. There are also several carbon fiber accents inside, as well as an aftermarket audio system. An Integra like this is obviously an acquired taste and won't appeal to everyone. But for anyone who grew up wanting a "2 Fast 2 Furious" build, it ticks almost every box, and it's being offered with no reserve, so it might end up going for cheap. This generation of Integra, which spawned a Type R that sold for $204,000, is also well regarded for its handling, so while the exterior and interior are a little bold, it should be plenty of fun to drive.

title: Starting Chess at 39 to Winning 3 Asian Medals for India: Ezhilarasi G’s Journey - ChessBase India
content: For most competitive players, turning 39 marks a step back from the tournaments, but for Bengaluru-based Ezhilarasi G., it was the beginning of an extraordinary journey. Affected by polio at the age of three, she discovered structured chess during the COVID-19 lockdown and, within four years, represented India at the 4th Asian Chess Championship for Players with Disabilities in Bishkek, winning one silver and two bronze medals. In her own words, she shares how determination and support turned a childhood pastime into an international podium finish. My name is Ezhilarasi. I am 43 years old, originally from Nathamalai village in Cuddalore district, Tamil Nadu, and currently residing in Bengaluru, Karnataka. I was affected by polio at the age of three, resulting in a physical disability affecting both my legs. Due to my circumstances, I had to discontinue my formal education after Class 8. Growing up in a small village, I had very limited exposure to the outside world. From the age of 14 until around 30, I spent most of my time at home. During my childhood, as I was not attending school, I started playing chess at home with my brother. At that time, I had no idea that chess could offer opportunities beyond simply playing a game. Gradually, I developed a special interest in it, little knowing that it would one day become such an important part of my life. Later, due to personal and family circumstances, I left home and started working with NGOs. I learned embroidery, handicrafts and other creative skills, and eventually began teaching these skills to persons with disabilities. During my work with an NGO in Chennai, I met my husband, Adarsh Edamana, at the age of 31. We got married two years later, in 2016, and eventually settled in Bengaluru. My husband has always been my biggest strength, encouraging me to pursue my dreams and supporting me through every difficulty. My serious chess journey began at the age of 39 during the COVID-19 lockdown, when I started playing again at home. I decided to learn the game properly. Since travelling to a training centre was difficult, my first coach, Karthik, came to my home and trained me for around three months. Later, I met with an accident and suffered a fracture in my right hand, but I did not give up chess. I came to know about the Chess Federation for Physically Disabled (CFPD), which supports persons with disabilities through chess. In December 2022, I participated in my first national-level competition at Tumakuru. There, I met Mr Anand Babu VL, Secretary of CFPD, who encouraged and supported me in participating in tournaments and selection events. I also met Coach NI – Dinakaran B, who has been training and guiding me ever since. Their support has played an important role in my progress. In 2024, I participated in the Tata Steel 4th All India Specially Abled FIDE Rated Chess Championship, held in Jharkhand, and secured first place in the Unrated Category with 5.5 points. I qualified for the 2nd Asian Chess Championship for Players with Disabilities 2024, held in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. I scored 6 points out of 9 rounds and secured fourth place in the women's championship. After that, I participated in a few national and international tournaments but could not achieve the results I had hoped for. However, I continued participating, learning from every experience and working to improve my game. In May 2026, I participated in the Chief Minister Trophy – 6th CFPD National Chess Championship 2026, held in Indore, Madhya Pradesh, from 27 to 30 May 2026. I secured 2nd Position (Silver Medal) in the Wheelchair Women (WC-Women) category. This achievement paved the way for my selection by the Sports Authority of India (SAI) to represent India internationally. My biggest achievement came when I represented India at the 4th Asian Chess Championship for Players with Disabilities, held in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, from 29 October to 8 November 2026. Being one of the nine players representing India was a proud moment. I was also the only woman representing Karnataka and the only woman above 40 years of age in the Indian contingent. I won three medals for India: Silver in Women's Rapid Chess and Bronze in Women's Blitz and Women's Standard (Classical) Chess. Standing on the international podium and representing my country was an unforgettable experience. I am deeply grateful to my husband, Adarsh Edamana, Mr Anand Babu VL, Secretary of CFPD, for his encouragement and support, Coach Dinakaran B for his continuous training and guidance, and Mr Tamil Arasan, our team manager, for supporting us and taking care of the arrangements throughout the championship. My journey has also involved financial difficulties. After COVID, my husband lost his job, making it challenging to manage household expenses and support my chess career. Due to financial constraints, I could not participate in as many tournaments as I wanted. Nevertheless, we have managed with whatever resources we have and continued supporting my chess journey. At present, I teach chess to a few children at home, helping them learn the game from the basics. This provides me with a livelihood while allowing me to share my knowledge and love for chess. Alongside teaching, I continue to train and prepare for upcoming competitions. My dream is to keep improving, participate in more international competitions and win gold medals for India. I also hope my journey inspires other women and persons with disabilities to pursue their dreams, irrespective of age or circumstances. I began my serious chess journey at 39, and today, at 43, I have represented India and won three medals at an Asian Championship. For me, chess is no longer just a game I played with my brother; it has become a journey that has changed my life. I believe it is never too late to start something new, believe in yourself, and achieve what once seemed impossible. title: The Best Matzo Ball Soup In Los Angeles Might Be Better Than Bubbe's - Tasting Table
content: The original Birdie G's in Santa Monica opened in 2019, and it was quickly recognized as one of the best restaurants in Los Angeles for its Jewish-American-inspired menu. When it opened, The Los Angeles Times called it "Santa Monica's hottest restaurant of the year." Later, the restaurant was named a Michelin Bib Gourmand. One of the signature dishes that earned Birdie G's all its accolades is chef Jeremy Fox's comforting yet elegant matzo ball soup, which some say is the best in the region. There are three key ingredients for traditional matzo balls: matzo meal, fat, and eggs. It's a seemingly simple dish, so what makes this matzo ball soup so special? Tasting Table spoke with chef Jeremy Fox to find out. The original Birdie G's closed at the end of 2025, but the restaurant recently reopened in Century City, bringing its beloved matzo ball soup to Los Angeles. To this day, the matzo ball soup is the dish that causes Fox the most stress because "I'm never going to beat that person's grandmother's matzo ball soup ... So I really work hard to make sure that ... the matzo ball soup is where it should be." Chef Jeremy Fox's matzo ball soup is richer and has more umami flavors than most — and he shared a lot of his matzo ball tips and tricks that make it so. First, he uses matzo meal from The Matzo Project in Brooklyn, New York, mixed with his house-rendered schmaltz, made by rendering chicken fat and onions. He told Tasting Table that the matzo meal and schmaltz are mixed with organic eggs and "lots of fresh dill," plus a little bit of baking powder. Fox takes inspiration from his grandmother's matzo ball soup, although he admittedly makes it in a different style. "Her matzo balls were very very light. Definitely floaters and ours are more sinkers," said Fox. The chicken broth, however, is labeled on the menu as "Rachael's chicken broth." It's named after Fox's wife, Rachael Sheridan, and is made using chicken backs, feet, and wings. "So it has a good amount of gelatin," he explained. After a cooking and cooling process, the stock then gets steeped with gribenes and dill stems. Fox said that enriches the stock and gives it a roasted chicken quality. The big matzo ball is served with some fresh carrots and fresh dill, and then topped with carrot miso. The stock is then poured tableside, melting the miso into the broth. From the dense yet still pillowy matzo ball to the rich chicken broth, and the umami from the carrot miso, this soup is the ultimate bowl of comfort.

The GS Explorer S beats the Apple Watch SE 3 on battery, GPS and water resistance, but lacks Apple's polished user experience. Back in October 2017, I took off my Casio G-Shock for the last time, strapped on an Apple Watch Series 3, and haven’t looked back. I worked my way up through Apple’s lineup until the Ultra was released in 2022. Today, I’m wearing an Ultra 4. Also: I tested the Apple Watch Ultra 4, and these 4 upgrades matter most Given how attached I’ve become to the Apple Watch, it’s rare for me to even review any alternatives (I gave the Garmin Fenix 8 Pro a go, but it wasn’t for me), so I was surprised to find how much I liked the sub-$300 Mibro GS Explorer S Titanium, a watch from a lesser-known brand. I got to test the titanium version of the GS Explorer S, but note there’s a cheaper ceramic model that’s virtually identical except for three things — the material (titanium alloy vs. ceramic and fiber-reinforced polymer), mapping (only the titanium version has offline mapping), and of course, price. The weight is also slightly different at 0.18 oz, but that’s small enough to ignore. To keep things simple, I’m not including the titanium version with the metal band in this comparison. Another feature that’s key to the success of a smartwatch is battery life. A few things stand out to me with this watch, both positive and negative. As an Apple Watch wearer, getting a couple of days from my Ultra is good, so I find going well over a week between charges quite remarkable. It eliminates that nightly charge, which I’d appreciate on those multi-day hikes where I’d normally take my Apple Watch charger. Also: Suunto Race 3S review: How real-time dynamic pacing improved my trail runs However, I’m so used to charging my Apple Watch nightly that it’s become a ritual, and switching to a weekly (or even less frequent) charging schedule makes it more likely I’ll forget. Also, it comes with a proprietary magnetic charging cable rather than a standard USB-C, which is a little more limiting. I suppose the good news is that if I lose it, there are replacements available. I like that it comes with two bands, which gives more options. I’m a fan of orange, so that’s my choice there. And, in contrast to a lot of smartwatches, changing the band is relatively easy because it uses a custom quick-release spring bar that can be opened with a finger. Nice touch. The Corning Gorilla Glass 3 gets a thumbs-up from me, despite being over a decade old. There are much worse materials to make a smartwatch crystal from, and I expect it to resist scratches, scrapes, and bumps well. For a rugged watch, the screen is the part most likely to get scratched, and decent protection is vital if the watch is to survive for any length of time. However, it’s not invulnerable by any stretch of the imagination. And I know from experience that it won’t be anywhere near as durable as the sapphire that’s on my Apple Watch Ultra. But that’s in a totally different price category. Another thumbs-up from me is the display’s 1,500-nit brightness, making it ideal for outdoor conditions. If you’re thinking of going for the titanium model to get your hands on mapping, know that the maps are limited to 31 x 31-mile (50 x 50 km) tiles, which explains the odd number. Also, while you get features such as route following, deviation alerts, one-tap return, and track-back navigation, it lacks advanced routing features like route creation and rerouting. Also: I tried a $200 smartwatch with voice recording – it beat the Apple Watch in a few key ways The mapping is also somewhat sparse. But remember, I’m from the UK and we have excellent Ordnance Survey mapping of the entire country down to 1:25,000 resolution at an incredible level of detail. So for me, anything that doesn’t show me everything from big boulders on my path feels sparse. Compare the mapping to what I can get on my Apple Watch from the mapping service in the Outdooractive app (iOS/Android). The Mibro Fit app is somewhat hit-and-miss, but it’s nowhere near as bad as the reviews made it out to be, so I feel it’s improved over the last couple of years. Yes, it’s a bit clunky and rough around the edges, but it did the job. There’s no point bothering with an outdoor smartwatch if the data you’re gathering is inaccurate or incomplete. When reviewing outdoor gadgets, conscious of — and clear about — the fact that I’m one person, and the best I can do is compare one device against another. So, when I was testing the accuracy of the heart rate, SpO2, and location data, I compared them to the Apple Watch Ultra 4. I tested the sensors while resting, walking, and hiking, and compared the data between the two devices. Two conclusions came from my testing: This is an obvious question that a lot of people are going to be asking, but it comes down to this: the Apple Watch is the clear winner, with one big, glaring caveat. From the apps to advanced health features, optional 5G, and built-in payment handling, not to mention safety features such as fall and crash detection, the Apple Watch is better… if you have an iPhone. Also: I tested the world’s first solar AMOLED sports watch – how charging works If you have an Android, the GS Explorer S is the better smartwatch. Compare this to, say, the Apple Watch SE 3, and you get better battery life (18 hours of normal use vs. 20 days), better GPS (single-band vs. dual-band), and better water resistance (164 feet vs. 328 feet, and the GS Explorer S is OK with diving to 98 feet). And if we’re comparing the titanium model, there’s mapping (although there are also plenty of mapping apps for the Apple Watch). It leaves the SE 3 in the dust. I could compare it to the Ultra 4 and say you get a lot of outdoor smartwatch for a lot less, but it’s hard to make a fair comparison either way, given the big price difference and how mature the Apple Watch ecosystem is. If you’re an Android user, the Apple Watch ecosystem isn’t on your radar, so the field is more open since flagships like the Pixel Watch 5 or Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 lean more toward being smartwatches than rugged outdoor watches (the exception being the Galaxy Watch Ultra). Wearables have to fit into people’s style and aesthetic, and what I like might not suit you, so I like to offer some options. Here are a few alternatives you might want to check out: Watches are tough to review because they are so personal. I like big watches, but you might like small ones. I like a lot of information on the display, while you might like the bare minimum. We’re all different. What I can say about the Mibro GS Explorer S is that, for the price (which at the time of writing is $140 and $230 for the ceramic or titanium models, respectively), it’s a very good outdoor smartwatch. Also: Flipper Zero vs. Flipper One: Why the new model isn’t an upgrade If this does interest you, give thought to whether you want the ceramic or titanium version. The key difference is mapping, but I’m not fully sold on it because the map tiles are somewhat small and the routing features are limited when you’re actually on a route. Knowing this might tip you toward the ceramic model, unless you like the titanium look. If you’re a fitness enthusiast, the GS Explorer S will give you all the stats you need to keep you on track, and more, for a very good price, and a device that should give you a good few years of service. title: GS E&C Wins 1.8 Trillion Won Mokdong Redevelopment Deal - Seoul Economic Daily
content:
First 'Xi' Brand Project in Mokdong New Town
Complex to Be Reduced to 19 Buildings With Large Central Forest
More Orders Expected in Yeouido and Gwangmyeong GS E&C (006360) has been selected as the contractor for the reconstruction of the Mokdong 12 apartment complex in Seoul's Yangcheon district. With the roughly 1.8 trillion won project in hand, the builder's cumulative urban redevelopment orders this year have passed 7.3 trillion won. If it also secures large projects in Yeouido and Gwangmyeong, where contractors will be chosen late this year, its annual orders are expected to exceed 10 trillion won and reach around 11 trillion won. The Mokdong 12 reconstruction association picked GS E&C as its contractor at a general meeting held the previous day at Dongyang Mirae University in Seoul's Guro district, according to redevelopment industry sources on the 23rd. It marks the first time the company's "Xi" brand will be used in the reconstruction of Mokdong New Town, which comprises 14 complexes. The project will replace 1,860 existing apartment units at 326 Sinjeong-dong in Yangcheon district with 2,810 units across 19 buildings rising up to 41 stories, along with support and welfare facilities. Construction costs total about 1.7887 trillion won. Mokdong 12 sits near Yangcheon-gu Office Station on Seoul's subway Line 2 as well as Sintree Park and Gyenam Park, giving it both transit access and green space. GS E&C proposed "Ripplize Xi" as the complex name, combining "ripple," "luz" for light and the suffix "-ize" to evoke the beautiful transformation of light and water. Under the concept of "building a forest in Mokdong," the builder cut the number of residential buildings to 19 from the 22 in the original plan and created a large central woodland. The complex is planned with 15 themed gardens and about 3 kilometers of walking paths. It will also adopt Clima, a future-oriented climate response system. Sensor-driven flood barriers that detect weather conditions in real time and operate automatically, along with modular rainwater retention tanks, are designed to respond preemptively to extreme weather such as torrential rain, strengthening the complex's safety and the sustainability of its living environment. An "all-in-one high-end community" will offer 60 programs spanning education, exercise, relaxation and dining. Facilities include the Scala Library, all-day dining and an indoor swimming pool, as well as a 110-meter "Scala Bridge" linking three buildings and a sky lounge. GS E&C has won 5.5477 trillion won worth of redevelopment work this year, including the first district of the Seongsu strategic redevelopment zone in Seongdong district, one of the year's biggest prizes at 2.154 trillion won, and the Songpa Hanyang 2 reconstruction in Songpa district at 685.6 billion won. Adding Mokdong 12 brings the cumulative total to 7.3364 trillion won. More orders are lined up for the end of the year. GS E&C has been named preferred bidder for the reconstruction of the Eunha and Samik apartments in Yeouido, Yeongdeungpo district, worth 1.067 trillion won in construction costs, and the Haan Jugong 12 reconstruction in Gwangmyeong, Gyeonggi Province, worth 1.2622 trillion won.
